question: How many golf balls are bought in the US each year?
clarify: Do we count only balls used on courses, or driving-range balls too? Assume on-course play; ranges are a small B2B add-on.
Are we counting balls bought or balls used? Assume purchases roughly equal balls lost, since golfers rebuy what they lose.
approach: US golfers (~25M) × rounds per golfer per year (~20) = total rounds
Total rounds × balls lost per round (~1.5) = balls lost and replaced each year

assumptions.label: US golfers
assumptions.why: Roughly 7-8% of the population plays at least once a year

assumptions.label: Rounds per golfer
assumptions.why: Blend of a few avid players at 50+ and many casuals at 5-10

assumptions.label: Balls lost per round
assumptions.why: Water hazards and trees; better players lose fewer

sanity_check: At ~$2 per ball that is ~$1.5B of ball sales, about the right order for the category leaders' combined golf-ball revenue.
so_what: A ball maker would use this to size its share target and decide whether premium or value balls drive growth.

question: Estimate the annual US market for dog food in dollars.

assumptions.why: Standard anchor

assumptions.why: Roughly two in five homes have a dog

assumptions.label: Dogs per dog-owning household
assumptions.why: Most have one, a meaningful minority have two or more

assumptions.label: Food and treat spend per dog
assumptions.why: ~$30-35 a month blending budget kibble and premium brands

sanity_check: Per US household that is ~$220 a year, or ~$560 per dog household, plausible for a monthly bag plus treats.
so_what: A pet-food brand would use this to judge whether the premium segment is big enough to justify a new product line.

Actual rounds per course = capacity × utilization (~50%)
Courses = rounds ÷ rounds per course

assumptions.label: US golfers
assumptions.why: Same as golf-ball problem

assumptions.label: Rounds per golfer
assumptions.why: Same as golf-ball problem

assumptions.label: Tee times
assumptions.why: Every ten minutes through daylight

assumptions.label: Players per tee time
assumptions.why: A full foursome

assumptions.label: Playable days
assumptions.why: Weather limits northern courses, southern ones play year-round

assumptions.label: Utilization
assumptions.why: Weekends full, weekdays and late afternoons thin

sanity_check: About one course per 24,000 people, i.e. a few per mid-size county, which matches intuition outside big cities.
so_what: A golf-course management company would use rounds per course to judge whether markets are oversupplied before acquiring.

question: Estimate the annual gross order value of quick-commerce grocery delivery (10-20 minute delivery) in India, in US dollars.
clarify: Top cities only, where dark stores exist? Assume the top metros and large tier-2 cities.
Gross order value including fees? Assume yes, converted at roughly Rs 85 per dollar.
approach: India population (~1.4B) ÷ household size (~4.5) = households; × urban share (~35%) = urban households
Urban households × share in cities with quick-commerce coverage (~30%) × adopters (~40%) = ordering households
Ordering households × orders per month (~6) × 12 × average order value (~$6) = GOV

assumptions.label: India population
assumptions.why: Standard anchor

assumptions.label: Household size
assumptions.why: Same as two-wheeler problem

assumptions.label: Urban share
assumptions.why: Same as cell-tower problem

assumptions.label: Covered-city share
assumptions.why: Dark-store networks concentrate in the largest metros

assumptions.label: Adoption among covered households
assumptions.why: Middle-class and affluent households in covered pin codes

assumptions.label: Orders per household
assumptions.why: Top-ups of milk, snacks, and essentials rather than full grocery runs

assumptions.label: Average order value
assumptions.why: Around Rs 500 per basket

sanity_check: That is ~2.6M orders a day across a few thousand dark stores, i.e. several hundred to ~1,000 orders per store per day, which is a plausible throughput.
so_what: A quick-commerce player would use this to decide whether growth comes from new cities or from raising order frequency in existing ones.

question: Estimate the annual US market for last-mile parcel delivery.
clarify: Last-mile cost only (depot to doorstep), not line-haul? Assume yes.
Parcels to homes and businesses? Assume both, with businesses as an uplift on consumer volume.
approach: Consumer parcels: US households (~130M) × parcels per week (~2.5) × 52
Add business-bound parcels (~20% uplift)
Total parcels × last-mile cost per parcel (~$5) = market

assumptions.label: US households
assumptions.why: Standard anchor

assumptions.label: Parcels per household
assumptions.why: E-commerce habits; some households get many, some almost none

assumptions.label: Business uplift
assumptions.why: Parcels to offices and shops on top of consumer deliveries

assumptions.label: Last-mile cost
assumptions.why: Often half or more of total shipping cost

sanity_check: 20B parcels is ~60 per person per year; the big carriers' combined US parcel revenue is in the low hundreds of billions, and last mile is about half of that.
so_what: A delivery-robot or locker company would use this to size the cost pool it could cut by batching or automating the final step.

question: How many Wi-Fi routers are sold worldwide each year?
clarify: Home routers and business access points? Assume both, with business as an uplift.
Including ISP-supplied gateways? Assume yes, they are routers too.
approach: World population (~8B) ÷ household size (~3.5) = households
Households × share with home broadband (~60%) = connected homes
Connected homes ÷ replacement cycle (~5 years) = home routers per year
Home routers × business uplift (~1.2) = total units

assumptions.label: World population
assumptions.why: Standard anchor

assumptions.label: Global household size
assumptions.why: Between rich-country ~2.5 and larger households in developing countries

assumptions.label: Home broadband share
assumptions.why: Many developing-world households rely on mobile data only

assumptions.label: Replacement cycle
assumptions.why: Upgrades for new Wi-Fi standards or ISP swaps

assumptions.label: Business uplift
assumptions.why: Offices, retail, hospitality access points

sanity_check: At ~$60 average that is ~$20B, a plausible size for global networking equipment sold to homes and small offices.
so_what: A chipmaker would use this volume to size the opportunity when a new Wi-Fi standard triggers an upgrade cycle.
